newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan's Export Finance Bank expands role in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's Export Finance Bank expands role in 1997.

text.p: Export and Finance Bank (EFB), Jordan's first private exporters' bank, said on Wednesday it saw future growth in tapping capital markets to fund industrial expansion.

The bank, in less than six months of operations, has acted as conduit for export financing from regional institutions to the country's leading industrialists and has also developed a growing commercial business, chairman Ali al-Husry said.
EFB, which began operations last August was the first Jordanian bank to be licensed since the late 1970s to service a rapidly growing export finance market.

EFB projects a 10 percent growth in Jordan's 1997 exports, helped by two major fertiliser plants coming onstream in midyear and a pickup in non-traditional exports. It said 1996 January to November exports were 934 million dinars ($1.3 billion).
Husry said EFB was now eyeing global capital markets for new financing channels for Jordanian exporters, having secured multi-million-dollar credit lines from regional export finance bodies.

EFB now has an agency deal with the Arab Monetary Fund's Arab Trade Finance scheme for cheap credit, and access to the Jeddah-based Islamic Development Bank's own credit lines. Both are covered by export insurance for inter-Arab trade through the Kuwait-based Inter-Arab Guarantee Corporation.
The bank's major shareholders include Jordan's potash and phosphates industry, the private Hikma Pharmaceutical Company, Nuqul conglomerate and another 1,000 shareholders.

Husry said the bank wanted to tap capital markets as its investment banking side grew, attracting foreign investment in private firms and helping firms tap global capital through corporate bonds and GDR listings.
No Jordanian firm has yet issued a corporate bond.
"I feel the future growth of the bank will come from project finance.. with a good stream of the business spilling from commercial to the investment side," Husry said.
EFB, in partnership with U.S. bank Merrill Lynch, was chosen by the government to advise it in the sale of a 26 percent share of the profitable state telecommunications body.
So far a "two-pronged" strategy has focused on commercial banking for a growing corporate client base and export financing credit deals from insitutions, Husry added.
"We are the first bank that has activated the Arab Trade Finance programme, so far utilising around $8-$10 million credit lines," Husry said.
Under the programme the bank arranged a $1 million deal to export pharmaceutical exports to Algeria and a $6 million line to finance raw materials for an industrial firm, Husry said.
EFB seeks a major role in retailing export finance offered by a $40 million World Bank package to boost Jordan's exports.
French export insurance company COFACE also extended credit risk cover to local exports in world markets, Husry said.
The Jordan Central Bank allows EFB concessionary long-term credit lines of up to five million dinars because it promotes exports.

The bank, with a paid-up capital of 10 million dinars, plans to double that amount by calling on existing shareholders in order to meet a minimum 20 million dinar capital requirement set by the Central Bank for all Jordanian banks.
The bank's first unaudited balance sheet shows deposits have grown to around 14 million dinars since the bank's formation. Its retained earnings of 215,865 dinars were put aside as debt provisions.
